tldr: This paper presents RoboARCade, a benchmark evaluating Agentic Robot Control (ARC)—where large multimodal models directly close the loop on robot control without intermediate programs—across 22 challenging, long-horizon manipulation tasks. Even leading models achieve less than a 50% success rate. The analysis reveals that failures stem primarily from poor approach strategies and sub-millimeter precision limits rather than visual scene misunderstanding, and that agents can dramatically improve through self-reflection and in-context successful demonstrations.
hero_caption: An overview of representative manipulation tasks in RoboARCade. All 22 diverse tasks—spanning precision biology lab protocols, physical puzzles, and tool kitting across single- and bimanual setups—are built on the MuJoCo physics engine with photorealistic rendering via Blender.
overview:
With the rapid advance of vision-language models (VLMs), robot control has evolved beyond training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies or generating code via Code-as-Policies. A new paradigm called Agentic Robot Control (ARC) has emerged, where the model directly observes images and iteratively outputs target end-effector commands in a closed loop without an intermediate policy. However, existing benchmarks feature short horizons or narrow initial condition variations, leading to saturated scores and obscuring whether agents truly understand scenes and control robots with fine precision.

To address this, the authors introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of 22 long-horizon, high-precision tasks across single- and dual-arm setups. Initial conditions are randomized far more widely than in prior work, and photorealistic rendering makes the environment genuinely challenging for frontier models. Everything runs on a single MuJoCo backend using modular data packs, making it straightforward to add new agents and interfaces.

Evaluating leading agents like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 reveals that even the top-performing GPT-6 Astra achieves only a 49.8% subtask success rate, leaving substantial room for improvement. Crucially, failures rarely stem from visual misunderstanding (losing track of objects); instead, they arise from poor grasp and approach strategies or a lack of millimeter-level precision. Furthermore, agents prematurely terminate and falsely claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks despite failing. On the other hand, providing just one successful demonstration in context (In-Context Learning) boosts Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0%, and having the agent autonomously write and refine its own textual instructions yields a comparable jump, highlighting a path toward autonomous performance improvement.
contributions: Built RoboARCade, a 22-task long-horizon benchmark tailored for Agentic Robot Control (ARC), where VLMs act directly as closed-loop policies without intermediate pre-trained policies or programs.
Systematically evaluated leading frontier agents (such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1) across two control interfaces, quantifying current ARC capabilities and cost-efficiency trade-offs.

Conducted detailed error analyses demonstrating that task failures stem from poor approach strategies, execution imprecision, and overconfident false success claims, rather than scene misunderstanding.

Demonstrated that agents can substantially boost their success rates without human input through in-context learning (ICL) of past successful demonstrations and autonomous text-prompt revision cycles.

sections.heading: Foundation models moving robot hands: Why do we need a new benchmark?
sections.summary: ARC allows foundation models to control robots directly without intermediate code, but prior evaluations yield conflicting results due to fragmented setups. RoboARCade provides a unified, long-horizon, challenging benchmark to uncover the true capabilities and bottlenecks of frontier agents.
sections.details:
Using foundation models (FMs) for robot control has advanced rapidly. Common paradigms include training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, hierarchical control where an FM provides language subgoals to low-level policies, and Code-as-Policies (CaP), where the model writes code that calls perceptual and action primitives. However, recent frontier multimodal models possess strong visual and reasoning capabilities, enabling them to inspect raw camera pixels and directly output target poses for the robot's end-effector in a closed loop. The authors call this Agentic Robot Control (ARC).

Prior studies disagreed on ARC's effectiveness: some reported success rates of just a few percent with direct control, while others showed over 90% using rich 3D visual interfaces. These discrepancies arose because tasks, models, and interfaces varied widely across studies. To establish a rigorous standard, the authors built RoboARCade: 22 long-horizon, high-precision tasks using single- and dual-arm Franka Panda and YAM robots, spanning biology experiments (such as loading PCR plates and centrifuges), physical puzzles, and tool kitting.

RoboARCade increases difficulty by widening initial object layout distributions and using Blender for photorealistic rendering. Evaluating state-of-the-art models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 showed that even the top model, GPT-6 Astra, achieved only 49.8%. Failure analysis revealed that agents rarely fail at visual understanding; instead, they struggle with selecting the right approach strategy and achieving millimeter-level precision, often falsely claiming success (24% to 39% of the time) when a task actually failed.

captions.F1: Representative manipulation tasks in RoboARCade. Across single- and bimanual cooperative setups, the benchmark includes over 20 environments requiring multi-minute assembly and experimental protocols, challenging agents' reasoning and precision control on a unified simulator.

sections.heading: The evolution of foundation models in robotics and where ARC fits
sections.summary: Robot control with foundation models has shifted from hierarchical VLAs and Code-as-Policies to ARC, where the model directly serves as a closed-loop policy. RoboARCade evaluates pure ARC settings along with the agent's capacity for autonomous, in-context improvement.
sections.details:
Foundation models in robot control generally follow three paradigms.

First is Hierarchical VLA: an LLM or VLM selects high-level skills (like SayCan or Inner Monologue) or handles reasoning and long-term planning, passing language subgoals to a low-level VLA policy—analogous to System 2 guiding System 1 in dual-process theory.

Second is Code-as-Policies (CaP): the model generates executable code that calls pre-defined primitive functions (such as object detection or grasp planners) to move the robot. During execution, the foundation model is not directly in the control loop.

Third is Agentic Robot Control (ARC), the focus of this work: the model itself acts as the control policy ($\pi$). It receives camera images and proprioceptive states directly, generating closed-loop controller setpoints (such as Cartesian end-effector poses and gripper states) without relying on external primitives.

Existing robot benchmarks (such as LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RLBench) were built for imitation or reinforcement learning and are ill-suited for multi-turn agent trial-and-error. Others, like EmbodiedBench, simplify perception by providing ground-truth 3D coordinates as text. RoboARCade directly tests an agent's ability to estimate 3D geometry from raw vision and execute long-horizon control. It also uniquely evaluates how far an agent can improve on its own through in-context learning (ICL) and autonomous prompt revision, without additional human fine-tuning.

captions.F2: Comparison of three foundation-model robot control paradigms. In hierarchical VLAs (left) and Code-as-Policies (center), intermediate policies or generated programs execute the actions. In ARC (right, this paper), the foundation model directly acts as the policy, sending commands directly to the controller.

sections.heading: An open, modular benchmark architecture and an autonomous improvement protocol
sections.summary: RoboARCade combines MuJoCo and Blender for photorealistic simulation, uses modular data packs, and supports flexible agent interfaces. It features a strict sandbox without privileged state access, along with protocols to evaluate in-context learning and self-refining text prompts.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Benchmark Infrastructure
RoboARCade is organized around three core components:
- **Simulation Environment**: All tasks run on a unified MuJoCo backend, rendering photorealistic RGB images with Blender at every waypoint. Target commands in the end-effector's Cartesian frame are resolved into joint position setpoints for execution.
- **Two Agent Interfaces**: The Visual Interface Agent (VIA) interface provides a rich visual environment where the agent previews and adjusts a virtual gripper in an interactive 3D point cloud reconstructed from multiple cameras before executing. The Multi-view RGBD interface is simpler, providing calibrated color and depth images alongside camera matrices, and executing relative translation, rotation, and gripper commands immediately.
- **Strict Sandbox**: Agents receive no privileged state (like ground-truth 3D object positions) or reward feedback during execution. They receive no external verification until they autonomously declare completion based on their own visual observations.

### 3.2 Distinctive Benchmark Characteristics
- **Long-Horizon Tasks**: The 22 tasks average 3,343 simulation steps (about 167 seconds at 20Hz), far longer than LIBERO-Long (276 steps) or RoboCasa (372 steps).
- **Diverse Embodiments**: In addition to single-arm Franka Panda, the benchmark features dual-arm Franka Panda and dual-arm YAM arms for bimanual coordination.
- **Wide Initial Condition Randomization**: Initial positions and orientations are heavily varied within valid physical ranges, preventing agents from succeeding through memorized open-loop trajectories.

### 3.3 Autonomous Improvement Evaluation
To test whether agents can improve without fine-tuning model parameters, two schemes are evaluated:
- **In-Context Learning (ICL)**: A complete past successful rollout—including tool calls and images—is provided directly in the prompt context before a new trial.
- **Multi-Stage Optimization of Task-Specific Prompts (T1, T2)**: The agent synthesizes a Markdown instruction manual (`harness.md`) from a successful trajectory, using it as a system prompt on the next attempt (T1). It then self-revises the instructions based on execution feedback and rubric scores (T2), and researchers track performance gains.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: Why agents fail and how they can improve
sections.summary: GPT-6 Astra led frontier models with a 49.8% success rate. Error breakdowns show visual misunderstandings were rare; failures were driven by poor grasp approaches and sub-millimeter inaccuracies. Providing in-context success examples or letting agents self-revise prompts raised scores past 70%.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra, all configured with maximum reasoning effort (xhigh). Each task is broken into subtask rubrics, automatically scored against simulator ground-truth states.

### 4.2 Zero-Shot Results and Insights
Analyzing task outcomes and execution logs revealed several key findings:
- **Q1: What causes failures?**: Classifying errors into visual understanding (identifying objects), approach (selecting grasp trajectories and orientations), and precision (aligning setpoints within tolerances) revealed that visual understanding failures accounted for only 2% to 6% of subtask errors. The remainder split evenly between bad approaches and precision errors (such as missing a 0.6mm insertion clearance by a few millimeters). Agents often recognized the error—noting that the gripper was off by 3–4mm along the negative Y-axis—yet failed to correct it.
- **Q2: Does trial-and-error help recovery?**: Retrying helps fix approaches and precision. For GPT-6 Astra (VIA), single-attempt success was 34%, which rose to 50% after five or more retries. However, recovering from a flawed approach is difficult; weaker models like Sol repeated the exact same flawed approach 76% of the time.
- **Q3: Do agents know when they have finished?**: Agents showed a strong tendency to believe an unfinished task was complete. Across attempted subtasks, Astra prematurely declared success 24% of the time, and Opus did so 39% of the time (Incorrect Success Claim).
- **Q4: Model and interface differences**: GPT-6 Astra consistently outperformed others, reaching 49.8% on VIA and 48.3% on RGBD. While the richer 3D VIA interface improved success rates by 1.5 to 6.8 percentage points over the simpler RGBD interface, it doubled tool calls and model turns, driving up trial costs by $1.7\times$ to $2.3\times$.

### 4.3 Autonomous Improvement Results
- **Q5: Does added context boost performance?**: Placing a single successful rollout in context (ICL) boosted Astra's average score from a 53.5% baseline to 73.0% on a five-task subset, largely by preventing agents from getting stuck in futile approaches until timeout. Furthermore, using a prompt autonomously synthesized and revised by the agent itself (T2) reached 72.0%. The text-prompt strategy avoids loading heavy rollout histories, significantly reducing per-trial API costs.
- **Q6: What persistent failures remain?**: Even with ICL and prompt optimization, three major hurdles persisted: extreme physical clearance demands, lingering false success claims, and poor improvisation when initial setups deviated substantially from demonstrated examples.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook: Tackling the real bottlenecks of agentic control
sections.summary: RoboARCade highlights both the promise and the bottlenecks of direct agentic control with frontier models. While visual understanding is largely solved, models still struggle with strategy selection, millimeter precision, and accurate self-assessment. Autonomous self-improvement offers a strong path forward.
sections.details:
This work introduced RoboARCade, a benchmark of 22 long-horizon manipulation tasks across single- and dual-arm embodiments, and presented a comprehensive evaluation of foundation models in Agentic Robot Control (ARC).

In zero-shot settings, the leading model, GPT-6 Astra, achieved just under 50% success. Detailed error analyses yielded a central insight: for frontier multimodal models, visual perception is no longer the primary hurdle. The real challenges lie in selecting kinematically viable grasp strategies (approach), achieving sub-millimeter alignment (precision), and objectively validating task completion rather than assuming success (self-monitoring).

Moreover, providing successful trajectories in context or letting agents iteratively refine their own prompt instructions elevated success rates beyond 70% without human intervention. This suggests that leveraging the autonomous in-context adaptation of foundation models may be more effective than engineering complex external control harnesses.

The authors note several limitations, including constrained task counts and random seeds due to high API costs, as well as a focus on quasi-static manipulation. Future work will look toward interfaces that output continuous trajectories rather than single-step waypoints, mobile manipulation, and dexterous multi-fingered hand manipulation.

takeaways: ARC—where foundation models act directly as closed-loop robot policies—remains an active frontier; even the leading model (GPT-6 Astra) achieves less than a 50% zero-shot success rate.
Failures in VLM robot control rarely stem from scene misunderstanding (visual recognition errors), but rather from flawed approach strategies and millimeter-level alignment imprecision.
Agents prematurely claim success on 24% to 39% of failed subtasks, highlighting the urgent need for better self-monitoring and verification mechanisms.

Rather than relying on expensive 3D visual interfaces, combining standard RGBD inputs with in-context demonstrations or agent-revised text prompts offers a far more cost-effective way to boost performance.
limitations: Evaluation scale and the number of random seeds were constrained by the high API costs of running frontier models across multi-turn rollouts.
Tasks are primarily quasi-static waypoint-based manipulations, leaving dynamic, high-speed trajectory execution unexplored.
The benchmark does not yet cover mobile manipulation with robot bases or high-degree-of-freedom dexterous hand manipulation.
